capital:撒莱.note: Built by Batu on the lower Volga after his western campaign, the capital of the Golden Horde, where the Rus' princes had to come to receive their patents.

capital:阿力麻里.note: A city in the Ili valley, the center of the Ulus of Chagatai.

capital:叶密立（窝阔台系）.note: The center of Ögedei's appanage, which Kaidu again made his base after 1269.

capital:马拉盖.note: Hulagu's capital, where in 1259 he had Nasir al-Din al-Tusi build an observatory.

capital:大不里士.note: Abaqa moved the capital here in 1265, and it became the capital of the Ilkhanate and a hub of trade between East and West.

capital:南京（东夏）.note: The capital Puxian Wannu built after moving east; taken by the Mongol prince Güyük in 1233.

capital:羊苴咩城.note: The capital of the Dali kingdom, backed by the Diancang Mountains to the west and facing Erhai Lake to the east, with the Three Pagodas of Chongsheng Temple as its landmark. Taken by Kublai in 1253.

capital:华闾.note: The capital of the Đinh and Early Lê dynasties, ringed by hills and water and easy to defend.

capital:升龙.note: In 1010 Lý Công Uẩn moved the capital from Hoa Lư to Đại La and renamed it Thăng Long; both the Lý and the Trần ruled from here.

capital:因陀罗补罗.note: The northern capital of Champa, abandoned in 1000 for Vijaya in the south under pressure from Đại Cồ Việt.

capital:毗阇耶.note: The capital of Champa from 1000, called "Xinzhou" by the Song.

capital:吴哥.note: The capital of the Khmer Empire; Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat (first half of the 12th century) and Jayavarman VII built Angkor Thom.

capital:蒲甘.note: A Buddhist city on the Irrawaddy with more than four thousand stupas and temples.

capital:开京.note: The capital of Goryeo. The Song envoy Xu Jing, sent there in 1123, described its walls in his Illustrated Account of the Embassy to Goryeo in the Xuanhe Era.

capital:江都（江华岛）.note: In 1232 Choe U forced the Goryeo king to move the capital to Ganghwa Island, which held out against the Mongols behind its strait for nearly forty years; the woodblocks of the Tripitaka Koreana were carved here.

capital:平安京.note: Residence of the emperor and political center of the Heian period, where The Tale of Genji and The Pillow Book were written.

capital:镰仓.note: Seat of Minamoto no Yoritomo's shogunate, the center of Japan's first warrior government.

capital:青唐城.note: The capital of Gusiluo's state, with Buddhist temples and crowds of merchants; a hub of the Qinghai branch of the Silk Road.

capital:萨迦.note: Home of the mother monastery of the Sakya school. After 1264 Phagpa was invested by the Yuan to head the Supreme Control Commission, and the Sakya ponchen governed Ü-Tsang on behalf of the Yuan.

capital:高昌.note: The royal city of the Qocho Uyghurs, who wintered at Qocho and summered at Beiting.

capital:于阗.note: The capital of the Viśa kingdom, taken by the Kara-Khanids around 1006.

capital:八剌沙衮.note: The seat of the Kara-Khanid great khan, a trading city in the Chu valley.

capital:喀什噶尔.note: The secondary capital and religious center of the Kara-Khanids, capital of the Eastern Kara-Khanids after 1134.

capital:撒马尔罕.note: The largest city of Transoxiana, capital of the Western Kara-Khanids.

capital:撒马尔罕（花剌子模）.note: Muhammad II moved his capital here after taking it in 1212; it surrendered to Genghis Khan in March 1220.

capital:布哈拉.note: The Samanid capital; the Mausoleum of Ismail Samani is one of the oldest surviving Islamic buildings in Central Asia.

capital:加兹尼.note: The Ghaznavid capital, where Mahmud built palaces with the wealth plundered from India; in 1151 the Ghurids burned the city for seven days.

capital:拉合尔.note: The late Ghaznavid capital, taken by the Ghurids in 1186.

capital:菲鲁兹库赫.mod: near the Minaret of Jam, Ghor, Afghanistan
capital:菲鲁兹库赫.note: The summer capital of the Ghurids; all that remains at the site is the 65-meter Minaret of Jam.

capital:德里.note: The capital of the Delhi Sultanate, where Aybak began the Qutb Minar.

capital:玉龙杰赤.note: The capital of Khwarazm, besieged for seven months in 1221 by Jochi, Chagatai and Ögedei; after it fell the Mongols diverted the Amu Darya to flood the city.

capital:剌夷.note: Tughril's seat after his advance west.

capital:伊斯法罕.note: The Seljuk capital under Malik-Shah, when the Friday Mosque was enlarged.

capital:梅尔夫.note: Sanjar's capital, called "the mother of the world"; its people were massacred by Tolui in 1221.

capital:哈马丹.note: The capital of the Seljuks of Iraq.

capital:设拉子.note: The capital of the Buyid regime in Fars, where Adud al-Dawla built a great library.

capital:巴格达.note: The "City of Peace", seat of the Abbasid caliphs. The Buyids and then the Seljuks controlled the caliphs; in 1258 the city fell and the caliph was killed.

capital:开罗.note: The new capital (the "Victorious City") founded by the Fatimids in 969, next to the old city of Fustat.

capital:开罗（阿尤布）.note: Saladin built the Citadel of Cairo and enclosed the new and old cities within one wall.

capital:开罗（马穆鲁克）.note: The Mamluk capital, where Baybars re-established the Abbasid caliphate in 1261.

capital:摩苏尔.note: The cradle of the Zengid dynasty; the Great Mosque of al-Nuri was begun in 1172.

capital:阿勒颇（赞吉）.note: Taken by Imad al-Din Zengi in 1128; Nur ad-Din made it his capital to unite Syria.

capital:科尼亚.note: Iconium, capital of the Sultanate of Rum; Rumi settled here after 1228.

capital:尼西亚（罗姆）.note: Suleiman made it his capital; the Crusaders and Byzantines retook it in 1097.

capital:阿拉穆特堡.note: The "Eagle's Nest", headquarters of the Nizaris, with a rich library. It surrendered to Hulagu in 1256 and the castle was demolished.

capital:耶路撒冷.note: The capital of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem; the Knights Templar made the al-Aqsa Mosque their headquarters.

capital:阿卡.note: Retaken by the Third Crusade, it became the de facto capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem and the busiest port of the eastern Mediterranean coast.

capital:安条克.note: The capital of the Principality of Antioch, stormed by Baybars in 1268, who massacred its people.

capital:的黎波里.note: The capital of the County of Tripoli.

capital:埃德萨.note: The capital of the first Crusader state, taken by Zengi in 1144.

capital:君士坦丁堡.note: The capital of the Eastern Roman Empire, "the Queen of Cities"; sacked by the Fourth Crusade in 1204 and recovered in 1261.

capital:尼西亚.note: After 1204 the Laskaris family founded the Empire of Nicaea here, carrying on the Byzantine succession.

capital:君士坦丁堡（拉丁帝国）.note: The capital of the Latin Empire; Hagia Sophia was for a time made a Catholic cathedral.

capital:特尔诺沃.note: The capital of the Second Bulgarian Empire, built on hills in a bend of the Yantra River.

capital:奥赫里德.note: Tsar Samuel's capital and the seat of the Bulgarian patriarch.

capital:埃斯泰尔戈姆.note: Where Saint Stephen was crowned; the Hungarian royal seat and the see of the archbishop.

capital:布达.note: After the Mongol invasion Béla IV built a castle on the hill on the right bank of the Danube, which gradually became the royal seat.

capital:克拉科夫.note: Capital of Poland from 1038 and, in the period of fragmentation, seat of the senior duke; burned by the Mongols in 1241, it was rebuilt under Magdeburg law in 1257.

capital:布拉格.note: The capital of the Přemyslid dynasty.

capital:维也纳.note: The Babenbergs moved their seat here in 1155, and Austria became a duchy the next year.

capital:基辅.note: "The mother of the cities of Rus'", where Yaroslav built the Cathedral of Saint Sophia. Stormed by Batu in December 1240 and its people massacred.

capital:弗拉基米尔.note: Andrei Bogolyubsky moved his capital here in 1157 and built the Golden Gate and the Dormition Cathedral; the title of grand prince moved north with him.

capital:不里阿耳.note: The capital of Volga Bulgaria, where furs from the north were traded for silver from the south.

capital:库塔伊西.note: The early capital of the Kingdom of Abkhazia and of united Georgia; Bagrati Cathedral was built in 1003.

capital:第比利斯.note: David IV recovered it from its Muslim emir in 1122 and made it his capital.

capital:阿尼.mod: Ani ruins, east of Kars, Turkey
capital:阿尼.note: The capital of Bagratid Armenia, called "the city of a thousand churches".

capital:特拉比松.note: The capital of the Empire of Trebizond, a trading port on the southern Black Sea coast.

capital:阿尔塔.note: The capital of the Despotate of Epirus.

pass:大散关.note: The northern mouth of the Qinling, commanding the Chencang road into Hanzhong; after the Treaty of Shaoxing it marked the western stretch of the Song–Jin border.

pass:仙人关.note: A gateway into Sichuan, where Wu Jie crushed Wuzhu in 1134.

pass:剑门关.note: The natural stronghold of the Jinniu road: "one man at the pass, and ten thousand cannot get through".

pass:武关.note: The southeastern gate of Guanzhong, leading to Shangzhou and Dengzhou.

pass:井陉口.note: One of the eight passes of the Taihang, the corridor between Hedong and Hebei.

pass:雁门关.note: On the western stretch of the Song–Liao border, where Yang Ye and his sons held off Liao.

pass:宁武关.note: A pass west of Yanmen Pass; its fortress was built in the Ming (1450), and with Yanmen and Piantou it was one of the "three outer passes".

pass:居庸关.note: The northern gate of Youzhou. Aguda entered Yanjing through it in 1122; in 1213 the Mongols could not take it and went round through Zijing Pass.

pass:古北口.note: On the route every Song envoy took to the Liao Central and Supreme capitals; Su Che, Shen Kuo and others wrote poems about it.

pass:松亭关.note: The main road from Pingzhou into the Xi lands and to the Liao Central Capital.

pass:渝关.note: Also written with the character 榆 (榆关); the eastern end of the Liaoxi corridor.

pass:瓦桥关.note: One of the "three passes" on the Song–Liao border; Song set up a border market at Xiongzhou for trade with Liao.

pass:淤口关.note: One of the three passes, where Song dug ponds and marshes along the frontier to stop the Liao cavalry.

pass:紫荆关.note: The Puyin pass of the eight Taihang passes; in 1213 the Mongol general Jebe entered Hebei through it.

pass:野狐岭.note: The strategic heights between the Bashang grasslands and North China, where Jin and the Mongols fought their decisive battle in 1211.

pass:克夷门.note: The northern gateway to Zhongxing Fu, the Western Xia capital.

pass:昆仑关.mod: between Binyang and Xingning, Nanning, Guangxi
pass:昆仑关.note: The pass north of Yongzhou, through which Di Qing marched by night in 1053.

pass:大庾岭.note: The Meiling road, the most important route between Lingnan and the Central Plains.

pass:采石矶.note: One of the narrowest points of the lower Yangtze. Emperor Taizu of Song built a pontoon bridge here to cross the river and conquer the Southern Tang, and Yu Yunwen drove back the Jin here in 1161.

pass:玉门关.note: The pass at the western end of Hexi.

pass:阳关.note: The pass leading out onto the Southern Route of the Western Regions.

pass:铁门.note: The gorge leading from Transoxiana to Tokharistan (northern Afghanistan), through which both Xuanzang and Changchun (Qiu Chuji) passed.

pass:开伯尔山口.note: The main road from Kabul to the Indus plain, by which the Ghaznavid and Ghurid kings invaded India.

pass:打耳班关.note: The narrow passage between the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus, called the "Caspian Gates"; Jebe and Subutai went north through it in 1222.

pass:奇里乞亚门.note: The pass through the Taurus Mountains from the Anatolian plateau down to the Cilician plain; in 1097 the forces of Tancred and Baldwin of the First Crusade went south through it.

pass:博斯普鲁斯海峡.note: The divide between Europe and Asia, whose southern mouth Constantinople commanded.

pass:萨列夫河.note: Emperor Frederick Barbarossa drowned crossing this river in 1190.

people:黄头回纥.note: Remnants of the Uyghurs who moved south after the fall of the Ganzhou Uyghurs, living south of Shazhou and north of the Qaidam; ancestors of today's Yugurs.

people:仲云.note: A people of the Southern Mountains (Altyn-Tagh) who claimed descent from the Lesser Yuezhi.

people:林木中百姓.note: The forest hunting tribes around Lake Baikal (the Barghut, Buryat, Qori and others), who submitted to Jochi in 1207.

people:蒙兀室韦.note: Living east of the Wangjian River (Ergune), ancestors of the Mongol tribe, who later moved west to the Onon.

people:两林蛮.note: Tribes south of the Dadu River, wavering between Song and Dali.

people:自杞·罗殿.note: States of the Wuman in today's western Guizhou and eastern Yunnan; Dali horses reached the Southern Song market at the Hengshan Fort in Yongzhou through their lands.

people:溪洞诸蛮.note: Tribes of the Five Streams region (today's western Hunan and eastern Guizhou), for whom Song set up loose-rein prefectures; the Peng family of Xizhou held office hereditarily.

people:黎.note: The Li communities of central Hainan.

people:播州杨氏.note: A family of native officials who had held Bozhou since the end of the Tang; it submitted to Song and at the end of the Southern Song helped defend Sichuan.

people:虾夷.note: Ancestors of the Ainu in Hokkaido and northern Honshu, outside the rule of the Heian court.

people:普鲁士人.note: Pagan tribes of the southern Baltic coast, conquered by the Teutonic Order from 1230.

people:立陶宛诸部.note: Baltic-speaking tribes, united by Mindaugas in the 1230s.

people:爱沙人.note: A Finno-Ugric people; after 1219 the north was occupied by Denmark and the south conquered by the Livonian Brothers of the Sword.

people:莫尔多瓦人.note: A Finno-Ugric people between the Oka and the Volga, conquered by Batu in 1237.

people:巴什基尔人.note: A Turkic-speaking people in the southern foothills of the Urals, absorbed into the Golden Horde in the 13th century.

people:瓦拉几亚人.note: A Romance-speaking people north of the Danube, dominated by the Cumans and Hungary and not yet organized as a state.

people:库曼人（匈牙利）.note: In 1239 the Kipchak chief Köten fled into Hungary with forty thousand tents and settled on the plain of the Tisza.

people:意大利诸邦.note: In southern Italy the Lombard princes, the Duchy of Naples and the Byzantine lands stood side by side until they were united in the Kingdom of Sicily after 1130.

people:库尔德诸部.note: Kurdish tribes between the Zagros and Taurus mountains; Saladin came from one of them, the Rawadiya.

people:阿拉伯诸部.note: The Bedouin tribes of Najd and the Hejaz, beyond the reach of the great dynasties.

people:也门诸王朝.note: Yemen was ruled in turn by the Sulayhids, the Ayyubids (1174–1229) and the Rasulids.

people:努比亚（马库里亚）.note: A Christian kingdom on the middle Nile, with its capital at Dongola, bound to Egypt by long-standing trade treaties.

people:拉其普特诸国.note: The Rajput kingdoms of northern India (the Chauhans, Kannauj, the Paramaras, the Solankis and others), which resisted the Muslim advance east.

people:波罗王朝.note: A Buddhist dynasty of Bengal, patron of Nalanda and Vikramashila; later replaced by the Sena dynasty.

people:朱罗王朝.note: A Tamil dynasty of southern India, at its height under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I (r. 1014–1044); it sent an expedition against Srivijaya in 1025 and repeatedly sent envoys to Song.

people:遮娄其.note: The Western Chalukyas of the Deccan, long rivals of the Cholas.

people:昔兰尼加.note: Eastern Libya, ravaged in the Fatimid period by the Banu Hilal, Banu Sulaym and other Arab tribes and controlled by nomads.

region:燕云十六州.old: Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun
region:燕云十六州.mod: today's Beijing, northern Tianjin, northern Hebei and northern Shanxi
region:燕云十六州.note:
Ceded by Shi Jingtang in 936 and handed over to Liao in 938. In 959 Emperor Shizong of the Later Zhou recovered the Ying and Mo prefectures and the three passes; the other fourteen prefectures were never recovered under the Northern Song.
In 979, after destroying the Northern Han, Emperor Taizong of Song pressed on to attack Youzhou and was badly beaten at the Gaoliang River; in the Yongxi northern expedition of 986 three columns advanced together and were again defeated at Qigou Pass and Chenjia Valley. Song then turned to defense, digging ponds and marshes and planting elms and willows along the Hebei frontier.
The Treaty of Chanyuan of 1004 fixed the border at the Baigou River, and Song and Liao kept the peace for 120 years. Liao made Youzhou its Southern Capital, Xijin Fu, and in 1044 made Yunzhou its Western Capital, Datong Fu; the Sixteen Prefectures became the richest Chinese lands of the Liao.
In 1120 the Song–Jin "Alliance Conducted at Sea" provided for a joint attack on Liao, with the Sixteen Prefectures going to Song. Song attacked Yanjing twice and failed both times, and it was finally taken by the Jin army; in 1123 Jin handed back only Yanjing and the six prefectures of Zhuo, Yi, Tan, Shun, Jing and Ji, which Song bought back with a "tax substitute" of a million strings of cash a year, renaming Yanjing as Yanshan Fu.
In 1125 the Jin army came south and Guo Yaoshi, commanding at Yanshan Fu, went over to Jin; Song lost what it had just regained, and the Jingkang Incident soon followed.
